Non-linear video editor · Linux

The edit you hear is the file you ship.

Kinetren is built on one promise: the preview is the render. The same composition, the same effects, the same frame — exporting just writes it to disk. Run the same project twice on the same machine and you get identical files, down to the byte.

Why it’s different

What you see ships

No proxy path, no “final quality” surprise at the end. The frame in the preview window and the frame in the MP4 come out of the same composition.

Same file every time

Render a project today and again next month and the two files match exactly — however much you scrubbed, looped or jumped around beforehand.

The timeline never stalls

Scrolling and zooming don’t touch your footage. Waveforms, filmstrips and poster frames are read from an index built once per file, so the view stays instant.

Your GPU encodes it

NVIDIA, AMD and Intel hardware encoders are picked automatically, with a software fallback that actually works. No temp files, no scratch disk filling up.

00:00:12

The edit

Video, audio and morph tracks, as many as you want, in any order — drag a track header and the whole row moves. Everything below is one keystroke or one drag away.

A reel from the middle of the edit, opened in place: its tracks right on the timeline, everything outside the instance veiled.

  • Cut and trimSplit at the playhead with S. Trim by dragging an edge — narrow clips keep a draggable middle, so you never lose the handle to the trim zones.
  • Regions do the workMark in and out with I and O, then use the region for everything: copy it, delete it, punch its interior out of every clip it crosses, loop it, render it.
  • Snapping you can let go ofOn by default, and holding Ctrl switches it off mid-drag. It catches clip edges, markers, region bounds, the playhead and zero.
  • Markers with namesM drops one and opens the name field. They sit on the ruler, drag with the mouse, and turn up in search.
  • Paste builds chainsCtrl+V leaves the playhead at the end of what it pasted, so pressing it again butts the next copy up against it — no gap, no seam, sample-exact.
  • Picture and sound stay togetherA clip and its audio move and trim as one until you break the link.
  • Find anythingCtrl+F searches markers, media, tracks, clips and bin groups at once. Ctrl+L jumps to a timecode you type.
  • Undo means undoEvery change, including morphers and bakes. A gesture is one step: dragging a clip across the timeline undoes as one move, not forty.
00:00:34

Playback

Transport you play rather than operate. Sound keeps the time and picture follows it, so nothing drifts on a long take — and the position you watch is smoothed between updates, so playback never looks like it is stepping.

Two speed bars

The top one holds a constant −2× to +2×. The bottom is a spring-loaded shuttle that snaps back the moment you let go. Drag past the widget and it finds a second wind, up to ±8×. Double-click either for 1×.

Hold space to run

Keep Space down and playback ramps up to 4× over five seconds, then eases back when you release. Tap it for play/pause; tap twice to stop at the top of the region.

Reverse, for real

Negative speed plays frame-exact backwards — audio too — and loops backwards past the region start. Individual clips can be reversed as a property of the clip.

Loops without the click

Region loops are continuous at the seam, not a re-seek. The head of the region is held in cache so the wrap never stutters.

Meters that read as meters

Discrete LED segments on a real decibel grid, a peak cap that decays behind them, and a master fader that reads out in dB. Scrub while paused and the meter shows the level under the cursor.

Preview on the other screen

Double-click the preview and it pops into its own window for a second monitor. Close it and it snaps back into the layout.

Ten video effects. The picker groups them by what they do and filters as you type.

Sound: two effects, one of them yours

  • GainA clean ±24 dB per slot.
  • Slowed + ReverbThe signature one. Slow the material down and let the pitch fall with it, then wash it in a reverb you shape with delay, decay, damping and wet level. Keyframe rate and mix along the clip.

Two details you feel rather than read about: the envelope is pinned to the material, so nudging an early keyframe doesn’t drag everything after it out of place — and the reverb tail keeps ringing past the end of the clip instead of being chopped off. Editing the clip next door won’t cut it short either.

Rate and mix, keyframed along the clip. Drag the diamonds; copy the envelope onto another clip.

00:01:02

The morpher

A morpher is a patch you drop on its own purple track. When you make it, it freezes the clips you had selected — and from then on it changes all of them at once, without touching a single one of them.

  • Swap the source under a finished editPoint forty cuts at the graded master instead of the rushes, or shift every in-point by the same amount. The edit — every cut, every duration, every position — stays exactly where you put it.
  • Push effects onto a whole groupAn effect batch appends to the chains of every clip it targets, and it applies live. Nothing to render, nothing to commit.
  • Delete it and it never happenedThe clips were never modified. Remove the patch and the edit is back where it started.
  • Bake when you’re sureBaking writes the patch into the clips and the block disappears — and the picture and sound don’t change by a single sample. It’s an organisational move, not a render. And yes, it undoes.

Six clips frozen in: a source swap, then VHS and Glow on top. Bake writes it into the clips.

00:01:16

Media bin

Drop files on the window and they land as cards. The bin is a place you arrange, not a list you scroll past.

Groups are named in a break in their frame.
Cards show a poster frame, the duration or a waveform.

  • Poster frames worth looking atEach file gets the most informative frame in it — not frame zero, not a black slate, not a fade-up.
  • Scrub without opening anythingSweep the mouse across a card and it plays through the file under your cursor.
  • Sound looks like soundAudio files draw their waveform right on the card.
  • Groups, named and lockedSelect cards, group them, give the group a name, lock it so nothing moves. Drag the group and it travels as one.
  • Free layout or gridYour choice, saved with the project — switching between them never scrambles your arrangement.
  • Drag onto the timelineYou get a ghost of the clip, a highlight on the target track and a snap line before you let go.
00:01:30

Export

MP4 — H.264 video, AAC 48 kHz stereo, faststart. Region or whole project, chosen by whether you have a region marked.

  • Encoders that are actually thereAuto tries the hardware encoders in turn and opens each one for real before committing to it. A card that advertises an encoder it can’t run gets skipped, not crashed on. Pick one by hand if you’d rather.
  • Quality your wayCRF or a bitrate target, audio from 128 to 320 kbps, output at the project’s own resolution or anything up to 4K.
  • Progress that tells you somethingWhich phase it’s in, an ETA, and how fast it’s going against realtime — minimum, average, current and peak. Pause it or cancel it.
  • Nothing leaves the appEncoding and muxing happen in-process. No intermediate files, no scratch folder, no gigabytes of raw footage written out and read back.
  • Render from a terminalA headless command-line tool renders the same project file, for overnight jobs and scripts.

One dialog: codec, quality, sound and container — then Render.

00:01:44

It looks after your work

Autosave that stays out of the way

Every 30 seconds — but only when the edit actually changed, and never in the middle of a drag or while you’re playing back. Written atomically, so a crash can’t leave you with half a project file.

Projects you can read

Plain JSON with relative paths to your media. Move the folder, zip it, hand it to someone else — it still opens. Your view, track names and bin arrangement come back with it.

The cache is just a cache

Waveforms and thumbnails live in a file beside the project. Delete it, break it, or replace a source file, and only what changed gets rebuilt.

Plain-language warnings

A performance panel with live cache fill, frames shown against frames dropped, and a notification when something is genuinely wrong — “decoding can’t keep up” rather than a counter you have to interpret.

Roadmap

Shipped

  • Multi-track timeline with regions, loops, punch-out and named markers
  • Ten video effects, chained per clip, live in the preview
  • Slowed + Reverb with keyframe automation
  • Morphers: batch source swaps and effect batches, with bake
  • Media bin with poster frames, hover scrub and locked groups
  • MP4 export with automatic hardware encoders
  • Headless renders from the command line
  • Autosave, atomic saves and portable project folders

Next

  • Titles and text on the timeline
  • Transitions as objects between clips
  • Colour correction: curves, white balance, LUTs and scopes
  • Clip fades, and keyframe automation for any effect parameter
  • More sound: EQ, compressor, de-noise, pan
  • More export targets: ProRes, WebM, image sequences, saved presets
  • Packaged builds: deb, rpm, AppImage and Flatpak

Direction, not dates.

00:02:26

Get it

Unpack the tarball and run the installer. It puts everything under your home directory — no root, no package manager — adds Kinetren to your application menu and registers project files so they open with a double-click.

# unpack and install
tar xf kinetren-*-linux-x86_64.tar.gz
cd kinetren-*-linux-x86_64
./install.sh

# or render from a terminal
kt-cli export project.kt out.mp4
Download for Linux x86_64
System
Linux on x86_64, glibc 2.35 or newer — Ubuntu 22.04+, Debian 12+, Fedora 36+
Display
X11
Video
FFmpeg 6, 7 or 8 installed system-wide. Kinetren uses the one you already have, along with whatever hardware acceleration it was built with.
Sound
ALSA or PipeWire
Installs to
~/.local — binaries, icons, desktop entry and the .kt project type
